title: Pearson VUE 5 Mar 2024
des: DOH (HAAD) paediatrics recall, Pearson VUE exam 5 March 2024

questions.question: A 7-year-old with asthma has had repeated admissions with acute severe asthma. He is now unable to talk in sentences and is short of breath. He has had inhaled salbutamol and his usual ICS (125 micrograms) without improvement. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Acute severe/life-threatening asthma not responding to repeated bronchodilators: give IV magnesium sulfate (40 mg/kg, max 2 g, over 20 min) along with oral/IV steroids and oxygen. LABA and ICS changes are maintenance steps, not rescue treatment.

questions.question: What is the most common site for intraosseous access in a child?
questions.exp: The anteromedial surface of the proximal tibia, 1–3 cm below the tibial tuberosity, is the first-choice IO site in children. Distal femur and distal tibia (above the medial malleolus) are alternatives.

questions.question: What is the main mechanism of action of adrenaline during CPR?
questions.exp: The α-adrenergic vasoconstriction of adrenaline raises aortic diastolic pressure and therefore coronary (and cerebral) perfusion pressure during chest compressions, which makes return of spontaneous circulation more likely.
questions.d: It converts VF to sinus rhythm

questions.question: A preterm baby on mechanical ventilation with PEEP develops feed intolerance and abdominal distension. X-ray shows a pneumothorax and air under the diaphragm, with no gas pattern of obstruction in the intestine. What is the cause of the free air?
questions.exp: In a ventilated baby with a pneumothorax, air can dissect through the mediastinum into the peritoneum (pneumoperitoneum without bowel perforation). The recall keyed the air leak. If the baby is septic or has pneumatosis, think of spontaneous intestinal perforation or NEC instead.
questions.a: Pneumothorax with air tracking into the abdomen (air leak)

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy cannot walk well and falls repeatedly. Several boys in the family have the same disease. He is on medication to improve muscle strength (steroids). He is referred to an endocrinologist to prescribe:
questions.exp: Duchenne muscular dystrophy on long-term glucocorticoids needs bone protection: vitamin D (and calcium) supplementation from the start of steroids. Bisphosphonates are added for fragility fractures or falling bone density, not routinely.

questions.question: A preterm baby is screened for retinopathy of prematurity. There is a flat, white demarcation line between vascular and avascular retina. What stage is this?
questions.exp: ROP stages: 1 demarcation line, 2 ridge (with height and width), 3 extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, 4 partial retinal detachment, 5 total detachment.

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl has abdominal pain, failure to thrive and erythema nodosum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Growth failure, abdominal pain and erythema nodosum point to Crohn's disease. Erythema nodosum is the commonest skin manifestation of IBD; coeliac disease is associated with dermatitis herpetiformis, not erythema nodosum. The recall marked coeliac.

questions.question: What is the most common skin manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum is the commonest (more in Crohn's) and tends to follow disease activity. Pyoderma gangrenosum is rarer and more typical of ulcerative colitis. Dermatitis herpetiformis goes with coeliac disease.

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa has secondary amenorrhoea. Which other feature is expected?
questions.exp: Anorexia nervosa causes hair thinning and loss, lanugo, dry skin, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia and constipation. (The recall also listed hypothermia, which is also a feature, so it was replaced to keep one best answer.)

questions.question: A 3-year-old adopted child has a fracture. Which fracture raises the most concern for non-accidental injury?
questions.exp: The recall keyed the supracondylar fracture. Be aware that the fractures most specific for abuse are classic metaphyseal lesions, posterior rib, scapular, sternal and spinous-process fractures; supracondylar fractures are usually accidental (fall on an outstretched hand), so any fracture in a young child needs a mechanism that fits the injury and development.

questions.question: A girl fell on her outstretched hand and has severe wrist pain. X-ray shows no fracture. What is the likely cause?
questions.exp: A fall on an outstretched hand with severe pain and no fracture: look for carpal dislocation (lunate/perilunate, with the capitate displaced off the lunate) on the lateral view, and for occult scaphoid fracture.

questions.question: A child has intermittent heartburn and now has dysphagia to solids, mainly meat. What is the best investigation?
questions.exp: Solid-food dysphagia and food bolus impaction in a child with reflux-like symptoms suggest eosinophilic oesophagitis. Diagnosis needs OGD with oesophageal biopsies (≥15 eosinophils per high-power field). The recall marked pH study.

questions.question: A picture of an infant of a diabetic mother with respiratory distress is shown. Which statement fits the definition of acute respiratory distress syndrome?
questions.exp: ARDS (Berlin/PALICC): onset within 7 days of a known insult, new infiltrates on imaging, hypoxaemia (P/F ≤300 or OI ≥4), and respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. (Options reconstructed.)
questions.a: Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload
questions.c: Onset more than 4 weeks after the insult

questions.question: An 11-year-old boy has no signs of puberty. His mother is 151 cm and had menarche at 14 years; the father had normal puberty. Bone age is 10 years. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Family history of late puberty with delayed bone age and normal growth velocity = constitutional delay. Note no puberty at 11 is still within normal for boys (delayed only after 14).
questions.a: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy has pubic and axillary hair, SMR stage 3, and symmetrical 5 mL testes. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: Enlarged testes (≥4 mL) with puberty in a boy under 9 = central (gonadotrophin-dependent) precocious puberty. In boys an intracranial cause is common, so MRI brain is needed. Small testes would suggest an adrenal source; one large testis a Leydig cell tumour.

questions.question: A 17-year-old boy wants a swimming scholarship. He is tall and obese (weight on the 90th centile), with bilateral gynaecomastia and small testes. Which test helps diagnosis?
questions.exp: Small firm testes, gynaecomastia and tall stature suggest Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY): hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism with high LH/FSH and low testosterone. Confirm with karyotype.
questions.b: LH (and FSH, testosterone) followed by karyotype

questions.question: A 5-year-old has polydipsia and polyuria. Two-hour post-meal glucose is 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L), serum osmolality is 292 mOsm/kg and sodium 140 mmol/L. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Normal glucose and normal serum sodium and osmolality make diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus unlikely; this fits habitual (primary) polydipsia. Reassure and advise. A water deprivation test is done only when osmolality or sodium is high or urine is persistently dilute.

questions.question: A girl with anorexia nervosa has an ECG. Which finding is expected?
questions.exp: Anorexia causes sinus bradycardia, low-voltage complexes and QTc prolongation (worsened by hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia), which carries a risk of arrhythmia.

questions.question: A girl with anorexia nervosa starts refeeding. Which electrolyte disturbance is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
questions.exp: Insulin release on refeeding drives phosphate (with potassium and magnesium) into cells. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark and causes weakness, heart failure and arrhythmia; check daily during the first week.

questions.question: A preterm baby has retinopathy of prematurity that needs treatment. Which statement is correct?
questions.exp: Treat type 1 ROP (zone I any stage with plus disease, zone I stage 3, or zone II stage 2–3 with plus) with laser to the avascular retina or intravitreal anti-VEGF. (Options reconstructed.)
questions.a: Type 1 ROP is treated with laser photocoagulation (or anti-VEGF)
questions.c: Laser therapy commonly causes exudative retinal detachment
questions.d: ROP is treated only after retinal detachment

questions.question: A boy with short stature had an operation for undescended testes in infancy. He now has small testes bilaterally and bradycardia. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Small testes after orchidopexy: start with gonadotrophins (LH/FSH with testosterone) to tell primary testicular failure (high LH/FSH) from hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (low), which would then lead to pituitary imaging. Check thyroid function too for the bradycardia.

questions.question: A girl has short stature and no menses. Neurological examination is normal and renal ultrasound is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Short stature with primary amenorrhoea in a girl is Turner syndrome until a karyotype says otherwise (ovarian failure; horseshoe kidney in about a third, though renal ultrasound can be normal).

questions.question: A 3-week-old has non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds and is hungry afterwards. Which blood finding is expected?
questions.exp: Pyloric stenosis causes hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid. Correct fluids and electrolytes before pyloromyotomy.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy has a hypopigmented (ash-leaf) patch for some months and a history of seizures. Which other finding is expected?
questions.exp: Ash-leaf macules and seizures suggest tuberous sclerosis; other skin signs are shagreen patch, facial angiofibromas and periungual fibromas. The recall described a hyperpigmented area below the axilla, which would fit NF1 (axillary freckling), but keyed shagreen patch; the stem is set as TSC here.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl has pleuritic chest pain, bilateral knee pain and a rash. Hb is 9 g/dL, platelets 100 ×10⁹/L and WBC 12 ×10⁹/L. Which test is most specific for the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Serositis, arthritis, rash and cytopenias suggest SLE. ANA is sensitive but not specific; anti-dsDNA (and anti-Smith) is specific and follows disease activity.

questions.question: A child has recurrent renal stones (renal Fanconi syndrome) and corneal crystals. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Nephropathic cystinosis: lysosomal cystine accumulation causing renal Fanconi syndrome, rickets and corneal crystals. Cysteamine (oral, plus eye drops) depletes cystine. Penicillamine is used for cystinuria, a different disease.

questions.question: A neonate has hypotonia, a round face, macroglossia and cardiomyopathy. Muscle biopsy shows glycogen. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Pompe disease (GSD type II): acid α-glucosidase deficiency with lysosomal glycogen in heart and muscle; infantile form gives hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, macroglossia and hypotonia. Treated with enzyme replacement (alglucosidase alfa).

questions.question: A child has hepatosplenomegaly and bone pain. Bone marrow biopsy shows lipid-laden cells. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Gaucher disease: glucocerebrosidase deficiency, 'crumpled tissue paper' Gaucher cells, splenomegaly, bone crises and Erlenmeyer-flask femora. α-galactosidase = Fabry; arylsulfatase A = metachromatic leukodystrophy; hexosaminidase A = Tay–Sachs.

questions.question: Which statement about long QT syndrome is correct?
questions.exp: Acquired QT prolongation follows hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia and drugs (macrolides, antipsychotics, ondansetron). Triggers vary by type: exercise/swimming in LQT1, sudden noise in LQT2, sleep in LQT3. The recall wrote hyperkalaemia, which shortens the QT.
questions.b: Hypokalaemia can cause acquired long QT
questions.c: Hyperkalaemia is the commonest cause of acquired long QT

questions.question: What is the most common congenital heart disease?
questions.exp: VSD is the commonest congenital heart lesion (about 30%). TOF is the commonest cyanotic lesion after the newborn period; TGA the commonest cyanotic lesion presenting in the newborn.

questions.question: Which ECG finding is typical of Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome?
questions.exp: An accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) pre-excites the ventricles: short PR, slurred upstroke (delta wave) and broad QRS. It predisposes to SVT (AVRT).
questions.a: Short PR interval with a delta wave and wide QRS

questions.question: An adolescent took 60 aspirin tablets 45 minutes ago and is symptomatic. What is the first step?
questions.exp: Activated charcoal within 1 hour of a significant salicylate ingestion (airway protected). Then check salicylate levels, give IV fluids, urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate, and haemodialysis for severe toxicity. Ipecac is no longer used.

questions.question: A teenager on treatment for depression is brought in with dry mouth, urinary retention, temperature 40 °C and tachycardia. Which drug did he take?
questions.exp: Anticholinergic toxidrome (dry, hot, flushed, urinary retention, tachycardia, mydriasis) plus risk of seizures and broad-QRS arrhythmia = tricyclic antidepressant overdose. Treat QRS widening with sodium bicarbonate.

questions.question: A child with ADHD, well controlled on regular medication and therapy with good grades, moves to secondary school and his academic performance drops. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: A sudden drop after a major life change (new school, peers, routine) in a previously well-controlled child is most likely emotional/adjustment stress. Explore it and liaise with the school before changing medication.
questions.a: Emotional distress related to the change
questions.b: Treatment failure needing a higher dose

questions.question: A preterm baby with RDS is given surfactant. Which complication is recognised?
questions.exp: Surfactant can cause pulmonary haemorrhage (falling pulmonary vascular resistance increases left-to-right ductal shunting), as well as transient bradycardia, desaturation and tube blockage during dosing.

questions.question: You are called to a preterm delivery. The baby, an infant of a diabetic mother, has laboured breathing; heart rate is normal. What is the best next step?
questions.exp: NRP/NLS: a baby who is breathing with a heart rate above 100 but has laboured breathing or persistent cyanosis should get CPAP (or supplemental oxygen as needed). Bag-mask ventilation is for apnoea, gasping or heart rate below 100. The recall marked bag-mask.
questions.b: Positive-pressure ventilation with bag and face mask

questions.question: A child had oozing of blood from the umbilical stump at birth and now has recurrent bleeding. PT, APTT and bleeding time are normal. Which factor is deficient?
questions.exp: Umbilical stump bleeding with normal PT, APTT, platelets and bleeding time = factor XIII deficiency (clot is unstable). Screen with clot solubility test or factor XIII assay. It also causes intracranial haemorrhage and poor wound healing.

questions.question: An X-ray shows a coin that has passed beyond the stomach into the small intestine in a well child. What is the management?
questions.exp: A blunt object past the pylorus in an asymptomatic child usually passes. Advise to watch stools and return with pain, vomiting or bleeding; repeat X-ray if not seen after 1–2 weeks. Remove button batteries and multiple magnets urgently.
questions.b: Watch the stools until the coin passes, with a follow-up X-ray if it has not

questions.question: A neonate in shock with temperature 39 °C and tachycardia has had two fluid boluses. Extremities are cold and mottled and perfusion has not improved. Which drug is next?
questions.exp: Fluid-refractory cold shock: start adrenaline (epinephrine) infusion; warm shock: noradrenaline. Consider prostaglandin only when a duct-dependent lesion is suspected.

questions.question: How is varicella transmitted?
questions.exp: Varicella spreads by airborne droplet nuclei and direct contact with lesions. Use airborne plus contact precautions (negative-pressure room) until all lesions are crusted.

questions.question: A ventilated neonate develops a pneumothorax. Which ventilator setting increases this risk?
questions.exp: Volutrauma and barotrauma from large tidal volumes or high inspiratory pressures, plus gas trapping with short expiratory times, cause air leaks. A long expiratory time protects against it.
questions.a: High tidal volume (and high peak pressure)

questions.question: Why are children with sickle cell disease prone to recurrent infection?
questions.exp: Repeated splenic infarction causes functional asplenia by early childhood, with risk from encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib, salmonella). Give penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal/Hib/meningococcal vaccines.

questions.question: How does hydroxyurea help in sickle cell disease?
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea raises HbF, which reduces HbS polymerisation, so there are fewer crises, less acute chest syndrome and fewer transfusions. It also lowers neutrophil count and adhesion.
questions.d: It acts as an iron chelator

questions.question: A child has recurrent Pseudomonas infections and a nasal ulcer. Which part of immunity is defective?
questions.exp: Recurrent bacterial and fungal infections of skin and mucosa (Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus, Aspergillus) with ulcers and poor pus formation point to a phagocyte defect (neutropenia, LAD, CGD).

questions.question: An infant has recurrent deep-tissue abscesses and disseminated BCG infection of the liver, spleen and lungs. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: CGD (NADPH oxidase defect): recurrent catalase-positive infections (Staph aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia, Aspergillus), deep abscesses, granulomas and BCG-itis. Diagnose with dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow test.

questions.question: A neonate's mother had no antenatal care. The baby has a rash, hepatosplenomegaly and now snuffles with copious nasal discharge. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Snuffles (rhinitis with copious discharge), maculopapular/bullous rash on palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly and periostitis = early congenital syphilis. The recall wrote rubella, which gives cataracts, deafness and PDA, not snuffles.

questions.question: A healthy child had diarrhoea and now has persistent haematuria, proteinuria and impaired renal function. Biopsy shows mesangial and endocapillary hypercellularity with thickened capillary walls. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Persistent nephritis with low C3 and a biopsy showing mesangial proliferation and thickened, double-contoured capillary walls is MPGN. Post-infectious GN resolves within 6–8 weeks; crescents define RPGN. Check the original wording; this was the recalled key.

questions.question: A child has leg pain, then cannot walk. There is a sensory level, a distended bladder, hypertonia and hyperreflexia. MRI shows demyelination of the thoracolumbar cord. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Acute transverse myelitis: high-dose IV methylprednisolone for 3–5 days first; plasma exchange for poor response. IVIG is first-line for Guillain–Barré, which gives areflexia and no sensory level.

questions.question: A child with cerebral palsy on mechanical ventilation has no respiratory effort, fixed dilated pupils and GCS 3, with HR 120. Which test is part of brainstem death testing?
questions.exp: Brainstem tests: pupillary, corneal, vestibulo-ocular (cold caloric), gag and cough reflexes, motor response in cranial nerve distribution, and apnoea test. Spinal reflexes may persist and do not exclude brainstem death.

questions.question: A child with a recent URTI has 2+ proteinuria and red and white cells in the urine. What is the next step to assess the proteinuria?
questions.exp: Quantify proteinuria with a first-morning urine PCR (excludes orthostatic proteinuria). 24-hour collections are hard in children and are rarely needed. The recall marked 24-hour collection.

questions.question: What should parents of a child with Down syndrome be told about sports?
questions.exp: About 15% have atlantoaxial instability (symptomatic in 1–2%). Routine screening X-rays are no longer advised; teach the symptoms of cord compression and avoid neck hyperflexion sports.
questions.a: There is a risk of atlantoaxial instability; report neck pain, gait change or weakness
questions.b: He cannot take part in the Special Olympics

questions.question: A 15-year-old has stage 1 hypertension (around 138/88) on readings at three separate visits. What is the next step?
questions.exp: AAP 2017: elevated readings at three visits should be confirmed with ABPM (excludes white-coat hypertension) before diagnostic work-up and treatment. Lifestyle advice starts in parallel. The recall marked medication.
questions.b: Start medication and review in 4 weeks
questions.c: DASH diet only and review in 1 year

questions.question: A child with cerebral palsy has excessive drooling affecting dental hygiene. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Anticholinergics (hyoscine patch, glycopyrronium) reduce saliva. Botulinum toxin to salivary glands and surgery are later options; speech therapy for oral motor control.

questions.question: A 3-day-old neonate has injected conjunctivae with copious purulent discharge. Gram-negative diplococci are seen. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum (days 2–5, hyperacute purulent): single dose ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg (max 125 mg) plus frequent saline irrigation; test for chlamydia and treat parents. Erythromycin ointment (the recalled answer) is prophylaxis, not treatment; chlamydial conjunctivitis (days 5–14) needs oral erythromycin.
questions.a: Single dose of IM/IV ceftriaxone plus saline eye irrigation

questions.question: A neonate has disseminated herpes simplex infection with deranged liver function. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Neonatal HSV: IV aciclovir 60 mg/kg/day for 14 days for skin-eye-mouth disease and 21 days for CNS or disseminated disease, followed by 6 months of oral suppression. The recall marked 14 days.
